original_value:
When an individual purchases a home, they simultaneously purchase its structural features, its accessibility to work, and the neighborhood amenities. Some amenities, such as air quality, are measurable while others, such as the prestige or the visual impression of a neighborhood, are difficult to quantify. Despite the well-known impacts intangible housing features have on house prices, limited attention has been given to systematically quantifying these difficult to measure amenities. Two issues have led to this neglect. Not only do few quantitative methods exist that can measure the urban environment, but that the collection of such data is both costly and subjective.
          We show that street image and satellite image data can capture these urban qualities and improve the estimation of house prices. We propose a pipeline that uses a deep neural network model to automatically extract visual features from images to estimate house prices in London, UK. We make use of traditional housing features such as age, size, and accessibility as well as visual features from Google Street View images and Bing aerial images in estimating the house price model. We find encouraging results where learning to characterize the urban quality of a neighborhood improves house price prediction, even when generalizing to previously unseen London boroughs.
          
            We explore the use of non-linear vs. linear methods to fuse these cues with conventional models of house pricing, and show how the
            interpretability
            of linear models allows us to directly extract proxy variables for visual desirability of neighborhoods that are both of interest in their own right, and could be used as inputs to other econometric methods. This is particularly valuable as once the network has been trained with the training data, it can be applied elsewhere, allowing us to generate vivid dense maps of the visual appeal of London streets.

result.paraphrase:
We examine how homebuyers acquire not only a property’s physical characteristics and commuting accessibility, but also neighborhood amenities. Some amenities, like air quality, can be measured, while others, such as a neighborhood’s prestige or visual appeal, are hard to quantify. Although intangible housing attributes are known to affect house prices, they have received limited systematic measurement because few quantitative urban-environment methods exist and collecting such data is expensive and subjective.

We show that street-level and satellite imagery can capture these urban qualities and improve house price estimation. We present a pipeline that uses a deep neural network to automatically extract visual features from images for predicting house prices in London, UK. In addition to traditional housing variables such as age, size, and accessibility, we incorporate visual cues from Google Street View and Bing aerial images into the model. The results are promising: learning to characterize neighborhood quality improves price prediction, even when applied to previously unseen London boroughs.

We also compare non-linear and linear approaches for combining these cues with conventional house-pricing models, and demonstrate that linear models are more interpretable, letting us directly derive proxy variables for neighborhood visual desirability. These proxies are useful in their own right and can also serve as inputs to other econometric methods. This is especially valuable because, once trained on the training data, the network can be applied elsewhere, enabling the creation of vivid, high-resolution maps of the visual attractiveness of London streets.
